SUBJECT: AB 1661 WORKPLACE HARASSMENT TRAINING FOR LOCAL
  AGENCY OFFICIALS

DATE:  NOVEMBER 28, 2017

BACKGROUND
On September 29, 2016, Gov. Jerry Brown signed AB 1661 requiring California mayors, city
council members, and other elected city and county officials to take a two hour sexual
harassment training. The legislation follows high-profile sexual harassment scandals involving
mayors of major California cities.

The provisions in AB 1661 largely track AB 1825, the 2004 law that requires California
employers to train supervisors about sexual harassment. The City of Palos Verdes Estates
further expands AB 1825 training to all of its personnel. This includes part-time staff, interns
and volunteers.

The Workplace Harassment Training for Local Agency Officials (AB 1661), is presented in a
format specifically designed for local agency officials including city council members,
commissioners and committee members and must occur within the first six months of assuming
office or commencing employment and then every two years after that.

The two hour training is provided by the California Joint Powers Insurance Authority and is
one among many valuable trainings to help identify exposures and to prevent losses.

TRAINING DESCRIPTION
The Workplace Harassment Training for Local Agency Officials will include an overview of
state and federal laws defining inappropriate conduct in the workplace, employer and employee
liability, investigation and appropriate action of a harassment claim, and prevention of
harassment claims. The discussion of harassment will include: quid pro quo harassment and
hostile or offensive work environment harassment.

SUBJECT: UPDATE AND OVERVIEW OF EMPLOYEE PENSION PLAN

DATE:  NOVEMBER 28, 2017

INTRODUCTION

The City provides a defined benefit pension to employees, and contracts with the California Public
Employees Retirement System (CalPERS) to manage the plan. Each year, CalPERS publishes an
Actuarial Valuation Report (AVR) for the City’s pension plan. The purpose of this workshop report
is to provide the City Council with an updated overview of the most recent AVR (for all pension
plans) as of June 30, 2016 (Attachments A through D) and the public with a primer on CalPERS
pensions. This report is to “receive and file;” it is for discussion and no action is requested.

BACKGROUND

The City of Palos Verdes Estates is like all other cities in the State facing increasing pension costs.
While increasing costs are significant, Palos Verdes Estates is not alone in this situation. Actually,
the City of Palos Verdes Estates is also and importantly in a much better situation than many other
cities. The City has no CalPERS post-retirement medical obligations (known as OPEB), previously
paid its side-fund of outstanding obligations, advance funded its unfunded liability to minimize
annual costs, and closely manage its overall operating costs to be in a better position. Past and
current City Councils have made strategic budget, staffing and labor agreement decisions to contain
costs. Cost increases result from CalPERS plans and decisions that are beyond cities’ control.

The City of Palos Verdes Estates and other cities cannot resolve increasing pension costs in any
immediate or easy manner. It will take, and is requiring, cost conscious budgeting, cities working
together, and constant efforts to address the issues with CalPERS to resolve the fiscal situation.
Reducing staff numbers (full-time positions) in a small city, for example, will not have a large impact
on reducing or eliminate costs. However, as long-time employees retire and new employees are

 hired under new pension programs, the CalPERS Board and State legislature implements structural
changes in pension plans, and the economy improves, cities are likely to see reduced costs. Toward

California Cities to monitor pension matters, personally engage with State officials and provide input
to the CalPERS Board.

DISCUSSION

Every City in CalPERS receives an annual Actuarial Valuation Report (AVR) from CalPERS. It is
a report on the City’s pension plan reflecting the employer’s contributions, plan assets, and the
financial information of the pension plan including both actuarial and investment assumptions.
Actuarial and investment projections for funding requirements noted in the report are based upon
actuarial assumptions, including investment returns and retiree mortality rates. The AVR sets the
City’s employer contribution rate for each fiscal year, and projects estimated annual contributions
for a 6 year timeframe. Within the AVR, there are 3 components:

    Contributions made by employees, deducted from their wages;
    Employer Normal Cost contribution; and
    Employer contribution towards the Unfunded Liability.

Attachments A through D is the AVR for all the City’s CalPERS pension plans as of June 30, 2016.

Employer Contributions

The “Funded Ratio” of the plan is calculated as market value of plan assets, divided by the present
value of accrued benefits. The goal is to have a Funded Ratio of 100%. The Palos Verdes Estates’
pension plan Funded Ratios at June 30, 2016 were 78% for Miscellaneous employees and 71% for
Public Safety employees. It is important to note that the Funded Ratios of the City’s plans incurred
a significant decrease in FY 2008-09, which was directly related to significant CalPERS investment
losses discussed below.

Cities, as the employer, make two different contributions into the CalPERS employee pension plans.
The first is the Normal Cost contribution that is for the benefit currently earned. When an employee
works 2-weeks, for example, the City contributes benefit equal to a percentage of wages for that 2-
week period. The percentage for “Classic” Miscellaneous members in FY 2018-19 will be 9.409%
of pensionable wages (base salary plus a limited list of other compensation payments such as
longevity pay). “Classic” Public Safety members have a percentage equal to 20.567% in FY 2018-
19. Fifty-two of the City’s 61 employees are “Classic” members.

The second employer contribution reduces the Unfunded Liability (UAL). An Unfunded Liability
exists when the market value of plan assets is less than the present value of the accrued benefits. An
Unfunded Liability is typically created when CalPERS investments do not earn as much as planned.
The employer contribution for the UAL is a payment toward the liability; and is expressed as a fixed
dollar amount, as opposed to a percentage of pay. The contribution is considered a legacy cost,
meaning a City must continue to make the payment regardless of changes to the workforce (e.g.
layoffs or wage reductions). The City’s UAL contribution for FY 2018-19 will be $719,646. If the

 City pays the full amount by July 31, 2018, CalPERS will discount the payment by $25,188 (3.5%)
to $694,458.

After FY 2016-17, the City’s total annual contribution is expected to increase by an average of more
than $250,000 per year. This is because the Normal Cost and the UAL increases resulting from the
reduction in the “discount rate” on plan assets. Seven years from now, the City’s annual contribution
is projected to be $1.250 million more than the FY 2016-17 contribution. The draft budget for FY18
-19 will include a cost increase of $255,000.

CalPERS Investments

The CalPERS investment portfolio totals more than $330 billion for more than 3,000 State-wide
member agencies. The investment earnings on this portfolio are critical to the pension system, as
they fund 62% of pension benefit payments and affect the UAL.

The CalPERS investment return assumption (“discount rate”) for FY 2016-17 was 7.375%. The
preliminary actual rate of return for FY 2016-17 was 11.2%. However, CalPERS does not always
earn such a favorable return. For FY 2015-16, the investment return assumption was 7.5%, yet only
0.6% was earned. Much of the Unfunded Liability came from CalPERS investment losses during
the Great Recession. To strengthen the pension system, CalPERS took action in 2016 to
incrementally reduce the investment return assumption (“discount rate”) to 7.0% by FY 2019-20,
thereby increasing employer contributions and reducing cities’ UAL.

 FISCAL IMPACT

Labor negotiations over the past few years, resulting in “Classic” members taking responsibility for
the employee portion of the CalPERS payment, has decreased the City’s current and future financial
obligations. Currently, in FY 2017-18, the City is paying a total of $1,245,000 to CalPERS for
pension costs. The required employer contributions for FY 2018-19 are expected to be $255,000
more than the FY 2017-18 contributions; however, with increased employee contributions totaling
approximately $100,000, the net increase in FY 2018-19 is expected to be $155,000.

RECOMMENDATION

The information herein is for information only, to provide an update to the City Council on the status
of CalPERS pension obligations and to provide the public with an overview of the CalPERS program.
Staff recommends that the Council receive and file this report.

This report presents the results of the June 30, 2016 actuarial valuation of the MISCELLANEOUS PLAN of the
CITY OF PALOS VERDES ESTATES of the California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS). This

Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS) was prepared by the plan actuary in order to:

  Set forth the assets and accrued liabilities of this plan as of June 30, 2016;
  Determine the required employer contribution for this plan for the fiscal year July 1, 2018 through June
  30, 2019; and
  Provide actuarial information as of June 30, 2016 to the CalPERS Board of Administration and other

should contact their actuary before disseminating any portion of this report for any reason that is not explicitly
described above.

Future actuarial measurements may differ significantly from the current measurements presented in this

and changes in plan provisions or applicable law.

Volatility Ratios
Actuarial calculations are based on a number of assumptions about long-term demographic and economic
behavior. Unless these assumptions (terminations, deaths, disabilities, retirements, salary growth, and
investment return) are exactly realized each year, there will be differences on a year-to-year basis. The year-
to-year differences between actual experience and the assumptions are called actuarial gains and losses and
serve to lower or raise required employer contributions from one year to the next. Therefore, employer
contributions will inevitably fluctuate, especially due to the ups and downs of investment returns.

Asset Volatility Ratio (AVR)

Plans that have higher asset-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return. For example, a plan with an asset-to-payroll ratio of 8 may
experience twice the contribution volatility due to investment return volatility, than a plan with an asset-to-
payroll ratio of 4. Shown below is the asset volatility ratio, a measure of the plan’s current contribution
volatility. It should be noted that this ratio is a measure of the current situation. It increases over time but
generally tends to stabilize as the plan matures.

Liability Volatility Ratio (LVR)

Plans that have higher liability-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return and changes in liability. For example, a plan with a liability-to-
payroll ratio of 8 is expected to have twice the contribution volatility of a plan with a liability-to-payroll ratio of
4. The liability volatility ratio is also shown in the table below. It should be noted that this ratio indicates a
longer-term potential for contribution volatility. The asset volatility ratio, described above, will tend to move

Volatility Ratios
Actuarial calculations are based on a number of assumptions about long-term demographic and economic
behavior. Unless these assumptions (terminations, deaths, disabilities, retirements, salary growth, and
investment return) are exactly realized each year, there will be differences on a year-to-year basis. The year-
to-year differences between actual experience and the assumptions are called actuarial gains and losses and
serve to lower or raise required employer contributions from one year to the next. Therefore, employer
contributions will inevitably fluctuate, especially due to the ups and downs of investment returns.

Asset Volatility Ratio (AVR)

Plans that have higher asset-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return. For example, a plan with an asset-to-payroll ratio of 8 may
experience twice the contribution volatility due to investment return volatility, than a plan with an asset-to-
payroll ratio of 4. Shown below is the asset volatility ratio, a measure of the plan’s current contribution
volatility. It should be noted that this ratio is a measure of the current situation. It increases over time but
generally tends to stabilize as the plan matures.

Liability Volatility Ratio (LVR)

Plans that have higher liability-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return and changes in liability. For example, a plan with a liability-to-
payroll ratio of 8 is expected to have twice the contribution volatility of a plan with a liability-to-payroll ratio of
4. The liability volatility ratio is also shown in the table below. It should be noted that this ratio indicates a
longer-term potential for contribution volatility. The asset volatility ratio, described above, will tend to move
closer to the liability volatility ratio as the plan matures. Since the liability volatility ratio is a long-term

  The hypothetical termination liability is an estimate of the financial position of the plan had the contract with

Volatility Ratios
Actuarial calculations are based on a number of assumptions about long-term demographic and economic
behavior. Unless these assumptions (terminations, deaths, disabilities, retirements, salary growth, and
investment return) are exactly realized each year, there will be differences on a year-to-year basis. The year-
to-year differences between actual experience and the assumptions are called actuarial gains and losses and
serve to lower or raise required employer contributions from one year to the next. Therefore, employer
contributions will inevitably fluctuate, especially due to the ups and downs of investment returns.

Asset Volatility Ratio (AVR)

Plans that have higher asset-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return. For example, a plan with an asset-to-payroll ratio of 8 may
experience twice the contribution volatility due to investment return volatility, than a plan with an asset-to-
payroll ratio of 4. Shown below is the asset volatility ratio, a measure of the plan’s current contribution
volatility. It should be noted that this ratio is a measure of the current situation. It increases over time but
generally tends to stabilize as the plan matures.

Liability Volatility Ratio (LVR)

Plans that have higher liability-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return and changes in liability. For example, a plan with a liability-to-
payroll ratio of 8 is expected to have twice the contribution volatility of a plan with a liability-to-payroll ratio of
4. The liability volatility ratio is also shown in the table below. It should be noted that this ratio indicates a
longer-term potential for contribution volatility. The asset volatility ratio, described above, will tend to move
closer to the liability volatility ratio as the plan matures. Since the liability volatility ratio is a long-term
measure, it is shown below at the current discount rate (7.375 percent) as well as the discount rate the Board

Volatility Ratios
Actuarial calculations are based on a number of assumptions about long-term demographic and economic
behavior. Unless these assumptions (terminations, deaths, disabilities, retirements, salary growth, and
investment return) are exactly realized each year, there will be differences on a year-to-year basis. The year-
to-year differences between actual experience and the assumptions are called actuarial gains and losses and
serve to lower or raise required employer contributions from one year to the next. Therefore, employer
contributions will inevitably fluctuate, especially due to the ups and downs of investment returns.

Asset Volatility Ratio (AVR)

Plans that have higher asset-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return. For example, a plan with an asset-to-payroll ratio of 8 may
experience twice the contribution volatility due to investment return volatility, than a plan with an asset-to-
payroll ratio of 4. Shown below is the asset volatility ratio, a measure of the plan’s current contribution
volatility. It should be noted that this ratio is a measure of the current situation. It increases over time but
generally tends to stabilize as the plan matures.

Liability Volatility Ratio (LVR)

Plans that have higher liability-to-payroll ratios experience more volatile employer contributions (as a
percentage of payroll) due to investment return and changes in liability. For example, a plan with a liability-to-
payroll ratio of 8 is expected to have twice the contribution volatility of a plan with a liability-to-payroll ratio of
4. The liability volatility ratio is also shown in the table below. It should be noted that this ratio indicates a
longer-term potential for contribution volatility. The asset volatility ratio, described above, will tend to move
